slides.title: What is a problem?
slides.text: A problem is something that is not working the way you want. If your block tower keeps falling, that is a problem you can try to solve.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your block tower keeps falling down no matter how you stack it. What is this situation?

options.label: A problem — something not working the way you want
options.outcome: Exactly right! A problem is something that is not working the way you want, like a tower that keeps falling down.

options.label: Not a problem at all
options.outcome: A tower that keeps falling down the way you don't want is exactly what a problem is.

options.label: A reason to never build towers again
options.outcome: Giving up isn't necessary — this is just a problem to work through, not a reason to stop entirely.

slides.title: Try a different way
slides.text: If your first idea does not work, try another one. If a tall skinny tower falls, you could make the bottom wider.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your first idea to build a tall block tower didn't work. What should you try?

options.label: Try a different way instead of giving up
options.outcome: Exactly right! If your first idea does not work, trying another one is a smart way to keep making progress.

options.label: Give up on the tower completely
options.outcome: Giving up means you'll never finish the tower — trying a different way is a better choice.

options.label: Keep doing the exact same thing that already failed
options.outcome: Repeating the same failed approach will likely give the same result — trying something different works better.

slides.title: Mistakes are okay
slides.text: Mistakes are part of learning. If your tower falls three times, each try can teach you what to change next.

widgetConfig.scenario: You tried to stack blocks and they fell over. What's the best way to think about it?

options.label: Mistakes are okay — you can try again
options.outcome: Exactly right! Mistakes are a normal part of learning and trying new things.

options.label: You're bad at building forever
options.outcome: One mistake doesn't mean you're bad at something — trying again is how you get better.

options.label: Never try building again
options.outcome: Giving up after one mistake means missing the chance to get better — trying again helps you improve.

slides.title: Asking for help is smart
slides.text: You do not have to solve every problem alone. If you are stuck, a grown-up, teacher, or friend may have an idea that helps.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're stuck on a problem. Do you have to solve it completely alone?

options.label: No — a grown-up, teacher, or friend may have an idea
options.outcome: Exactly right! You do not have to solve every problem alone — if you are stuck, a grown-up, teacher, or friend may have an idea that helps.

options.label: Yes, you must always solve everything alone
options.outcome: You don't have to always solve things alone — a grown-up, teacher, or friend may have an idea that helps.

options.label: Asking for help is never a smart idea
options.outcome: Asking for help is actually a smart idea — it can bring an idea that helps you solve the problem.

slides.title: Small steps first
slides.text: Big jobs feel easier when you do one small part at a time. If your room is messy, start by putting away just the books.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your room is really messy. What makes this big job feel easier?

options.label: Doing one small part at a time, like putting away books
options.outcome: Exactly right! Big jobs feel easier when you do one small part at a time.

options.label: Trying to do everything at once
options.outcome: Trying to do everything at once can feel overwhelming — doing one small part at a time is easier.

options.label: Small steps never make a big job easier
options.outcome: Small steps actually make a big job a lot easier — they break it into manageable parts.

slides.title: Celebrate figuring it out
slides.text: When you solve a problem, notice what you did well. You can say, “I kept trying, and I figured it out!”

widgetConfig.scenario: You solved a tricky problem. What should you do?

options.label: Notice what you did well, like "I kept trying!"
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you solve a problem, notice what you did well — you can say, 'I kept trying, and I figured it out!'

options.label: Ignore it and move on without noticing
options.outcome: Moving on without noticing misses a chance to recognize what you did well — celebrating helps you remember what worked.

options.label: Celebrating solving a problem never matters
options.outcome: Celebrating actually matters — noticing what you did well helps you remember what worked.

slides.title: A broken toy
slides.text: If a toy breaks, first look at what is wrong. You might be able to fix a simple part, or you can ask a grown-up for help.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your favorite toy stopped working. What's the best first step?

options.label: Look closely to see what might be wrong
options.outcome: Great first step! Looking closely before doing anything else helps you actually understand the problem.

options.label: Give up and throw it away right away
options.outcome: Giving up immediately means you might miss an easy fix, like a loose battery or part.

options.label: Hit it to try to make it work
options.outcome: That could break it more! Looking closely first is a safer way to figure out what's wrong.

slides.title: Take a breath
slides.text: Hard problems can make you feel upset. Take a slow breath, calm your body, and then decide what to try next.

widgetConfig.scenario: A hard problem is making you feel upset. What helps?

options.label: Take a slow breath and calm your body
options.outcome: Exactly right! Take a slow breath, calm your body, and then decide what to try next.

options.label: Stay upset and give up immediately
options.outcome: Staying upset and giving up doesn't help solve the problem — taking a breath to calm down helps you decide what to try next.

options.label: Breathing never helps you feel calmer
options.outcome: Breathing actually helps a lot — it calms your body so you can decide what to try next.

slides.title: Going slow helps
slides.text: Going slowly gives your brain time to notice things. If you rush a puzzle, you may miss the piece that fits.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're rushing through a puzzle. What might you miss?

options.label: The piece that actually fits
options.outcome: Exactly right! Going slowly gives your brain time to notice things — if you rush a puzzle, you may miss the piece that fits.

options.label: Nothing — rushing never causes you to miss anything
options.outcome: Rushing actually can cause you to miss things, like the puzzle piece that fits.

options.label: Going slow never actually helps you notice things
options.outcome: Going slow actually helps a lot — it gives your brain time to notice important details.

slides.title: Practice makes it easier
slides.text: Things that feel hard can get easier with practice. Tying your shoes may take many tries before your hands remember what to do.

widgetConfig.scenario: Tying your shoes feels really hard at first. What helps it get easier?

options.label: Practicing many times
options.outcome: Exactly right! Things that feel hard can get easier with practice — tying your shoes may take many tries before your hands remember what to do.

options.label: Giving up after the first try
options.outcome: Giving up after the first try means you never get the practice that makes it easier.

options.label: Practice never actually makes something easier
options.outcome: Practice actually does make things easier — your hands remember what to do after many tries.

quiz.question: What is a "problem"?
choices: Something that needs fixing
Something that is already perfect
quiz.explanation: A problem is something that needs attention or a solution. If a puzzle piece will not fit, first notice the problem, then try a different piece or turn it around.

quiz.question: Your tower keeps falling. What should you try?
choices: A different way
Keep using the same way without changing anything
quiz.explanation: Try changing one thing instead of repeating the same move. A wider block at the bottom may make the tower steadier.

quiz.question: Is it okay to make mistakes?
choices: Yes, mistakes are okay
No, stop if it does not work the first time
quiz.explanation: Yes. Mistakes show you what to change. If your tower falls, you can learn that the bottom needs to be wider or stronger.

quiz.question: You feel stuck. What can you do?
choices: Ask for help
Keep struggling alone even when you are stuck
quiz.explanation: Asking for help is part of problem solving. Someone else may notice an idea or clue you have not seen yet.

quiz.question: How can a messy room feel less big?
choices: Do one small step at a time
Try to do it all at once
quiz.explanation: Break the job into tiny parts. Put away the books first, then the blocks, then the clothes.

quiz.question: You finally fix your tower. What should you do?
choices: Ignore the effort you made
Feel proud of yourself
quiz.explanation: Notice your effort and feel proud. You did not only build a tower—you practiced staying with a problem until you solved it.

quiz.question: Your toy breaks. What can you do?
choices: Try to fix it or ask for help
Give up before checking whether it can be fixed
quiz.explanation: Check what is wrong before giving up. A loose wheel may be easy to fix, while a harder repair may need a grown-up.

quiz.question: You feel upset about a problem. What should you do first?
choices: Keep trying while you are very upset
Take a deep breath
quiz.explanation: A slow breath helps your body calm down so your brain can think more clearly about what to try next.

quiz.question: Why can going slow help you?
choices: It helps you make fewer mistakes
Rushing is better because you finish sooner
quiz.explanation: Going slowly helps you notice details. When you rush a puzzle, you can easily miss the piece that fits.

quiz.question: Why does practice help with problems?
choices: Practice only helps with things that are already easy
It makes problems easier over time
quiz.explanation: Practice helps your brain and body remember what works. Tying shoes feels easier after many tries because the steps become more familiar.

slides.title: Sorting and matching
slides.text: Sorting means putting things that belong together into groups. Matching socks by color or size helps you practice noticing what is the same and what is different.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have a pile of socks in different colors. What helps you organize them?

options.label: Sorting and matching them by color
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sorting means putting things that belong together into groups — matching socks by color or size helps you practice noticing what is the same and different.

options.label: Leaving them in one big random pile
options.outcome: Leaving them in a random pile doesn't organize anything — sorting and matching by color helps.

options.label: Sorting never helps you notice what is the same or different
options.outcome: Sorting actually helps you practice noticing what's the same and what's different.

slides.title: One step at a time
slides.text: You do not have to solve a big problem all at once. Ask yourself, “What is the next small thing I can do?”

widgetConfig.scenario: You have a big pile of laundry to fold and it feels overwhelming. What's a good way to start?

options.label: Fold one piece at a time instead of worrying about the whole pile
options.outcome: Exactly! Taking it one step at a time makes a big task feel much more manageable.

options.label: Try to fold everything all at once in one motion
options.outcome: Trying to do everything at once can feel overwhelming — one step at a time works much better.

options.label: Give up because the pile looks too big
options.outcome: The pile looks big, but taking it one piece at a time makes it totally doable.

slides.title: Think of a few ideas
slides.text: Before choosing what to do, think of two or three ideas. Then pick one to try first.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your tower of blocks keeps falling over. Instead of just trying the exact same way again, what's a smarter approach?

options.label: Think of a few different ideas to try, like a wider base
options.outcome: Great thinking! Trying different ideas instead of repeating the same thing gives you a better chance of success.

options.label: Keep doing the exact same thing again
options.outcome: If it didn't work before, trying the exact same thing again probably won't work either — thinking of a new idea helps more.

options.label: Give up on building towers
options.outcome: You don't have to give up — thinking of a different idea to try is a great problem-solving step.

slides.title: What did you learn?
slides.text: After something goes wrong, ask, “What can I learn from that?” If your drink spills, you might decide to carry the cup with two hands next time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your drink spills. What's a helpful question to ask yourself?

options.label: "What can I learn from that?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! After something goes wrong, asking what you can learn from it, like carrying a cup with two hands next time, helps.

options.label: Nothing — spills never teach you anything
options.outcome: Spills actually can teach you something useful, like a better way to carry a cup next time.

options.label: Asking what you learned never actually helps next time
options.outcome: Asking what you learned actually helps a lot — it can change what you do differently next time.

slides.title: Keep trying
slides.text: If the first try does not work, that does not mean you cannot solve it. Change one thing and try again.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your first try at something doesn't work. Does this mean you can't solve it?

options.label: No — change one thing and try again
options.outcome: Exactly right! If the first try does not work, that does not mean you cannot solve it — change one thing and try again.

options.label: Yes, one failed try means it is impossible
options.outcome: One failed try doesn't mean it's impossible — changing one thing and trying again often works.

options.label: Trying again after a failed attempt never helps
options.outcome: Trying again after a failed attempt actually helps a lot, especially if you change something first.

slides.title: Look closely first
slides.text: Before you act, look carefully. Small details can give you clues about what is happening.

widgetConfig.scenario: Something unexpected is happening. What should you do before acting?

options.label: Look carefully for clues
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before you act, look carefully — small details can give you clues about what is happening.

options.label: Act right away without looking
options.outcome: Acting right away without looking can mean missing important clues — looking carefully first helps.

options.label: Looking closely never reveals any clues
options.outcome: Looking closely actually can reveal important clues about what's happening.

slides.title: Follow the clues
slides.text: Clues are little signs that help you figure something out. If you cannot find your toy car, looking for where you last played with it is a clue.

widgetConfig.scenario: You can't find your toy car. What's a smart way to figure out where it might be?

options.label: Look for clues, like where you played with it last
options.outcome: Exactly! Following clues, like where you last played, helps you figure out where to look.

options.label: Just give up looking
options.outcome: Giving up means you'll never find it — following clues about where you last had it helps you figure out where to search.

options.label: Assume it's gone forever
options.outcome: Assuming it's gone skips the clues that could help you find it — think about where you played with it last.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Give yourself a moment to think before doing something. If you need to reach a toy on a shelf, first think about the safest way to get help.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to reach a toy on a high shelf. What should you do first?

options.label: Think about the safest way to get help
options.outcome: Exactly right! Give yourself a moment to think before doing something — like thinking about the safest way to get help reaching a high shelf.

options.label: Climb up right away with no thought
options.outcome: Climbing up right away with no thought can be unsafe — thinking first about the safest way helps.

options.label: Thinking before you act never actually helps
options.outcome: Thinking before you act actually helps a lot, especially for safety.

slides.title: Ask "why"
slides.text: Asking “why?” helps you understand what caused a problem. If a balloon popped, you can look for something sharp that may have touched it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A balloon just popped. What question helps you understand what happened?

options.label: "Why did that happen?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Asking 'why?' helps you understand what caused a problem, like looking for something sharp that touched the balloon.

options.label: No question is needed — just move on
options.outcome: Just moving on skips understanding what happened — asking why helps you figure out the cause.

options.label: Asking why never helps you understand a problem
options.outcome: Asking why actually helps a lot — it's exactly how you figure out what caused something.

slides.title: Toy cleanup sort
slides.text: Grouping similar toys makes cleanup easier. Cars can go in one bin, blocks in another, and stuffed animals in a basket.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have cars, blocks, and stuffed animals all mixed together. What makes cleanup easier?

options.label: Grouping similar toys together
options.outcome: Exactly right! Grouping similar toys makes cleanup easier — cars can go in one bin, blocks in another, and stuffed animals in a basket.

options.label: Leaving everything mixed together
options.outcome: Leaving everything mixed together makes cleanup harder — grouping similar toys together is easier.

options.label: Grouping similar toys never makes cleanup easier
options.outcome: Grouping similar toys actually makes cleanup a lot easier.

quiz.question: What do you practice when you match socks?
choices: Noticing what goes together
Only learning the names of colors
quiz.explanation: Matching socks means finding pairs that look the same. That helps you notice patterns, like sorting red socks together.

quiz.question: Before you try to fix something, what should you do?
choices: Choose before thinking of any other ideas
Think of a few ideas first
quiz.explanation: Thinking of a few ideas first helps you pick the best one, like using a stool to reach a shelf.

quiz.question: After a mistake, what is a good question to ask?
choices: What can I learn from this?
Who can I blame for this?
quiz.explanation: Asking what you can learn helps you do better next time, like holding a cup with two hands after a spill.

quiz.question: Your first try does not work. What should you do?
choices: Try one more time
Stop after the first attempt
quiz.explanation: Trying again is how you solve problems. Maybe your next tower will stand up tall.

quiz.question: You cannot find your favorite toy. What should you do first?
choices: Look closely for small clues
Wait and hope the toy appears
quiz.explanation: Looking closely helps you spot small clues. A toy car's wheel peeking out can show you where it rolled.

quiz.question: Your snack is missing. What can crumbs on the floor help you do?
choices: Find out who took it
Clean them up without thinking about what they show
quiz.explanation: Crumbs on the floor are a clue, like a trail leading to who ate your cookie. Clues help you solve a mystery.

quiz.question: Before you grab a tool, what should you do?
choices: Choose the closest tool first
Think about what you need it for
quiz.explanation: Thinking first helps you pick the right tool, like a spoon instead of a fork for soup.

quiz.question: A balloon pops. What is a good question to ask?
choices: Why did that happen?
Ignore what happened without checking
quiz.explanation: Asking why helps you understand what happened. Maybe the balloon touched something sharp, like a pointy toy.

quiz.question: How can you clean up toys faster?
choices: Put similar toys into groups
Put toys away without sorting them
quiz.explanation: Putting toys into groups, like all the cars in one bin, makes cleanup much faster.

quiz.question: You do not have to solve a big job all at once. What should you do?
choices: Do the next small step
Rush through the whole job at once
quiz.explanation: A big job feels smaller in small steps, like cleaning one shelf before moving to the next.

slides.title: Understanding the real problem
slides.text: Before fixing something, make sure you know what is really wrong. A toy robot that will not move might be broken, but it might simply need fresh batteries.

widgetConfig.scenario: A toy robot won't move. Is it definitely broken?

options.label: Not necessarily — it might just need fresh batteries
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before fixing something, make sure you know what is really wrong — a toy robot that won't move might simply need fresh batteries.

options.label: Yes, it is definitely broken for good
options.outcome: It's not necessarily broken for good — it might just need fresh batteries.

options.label: Understanding what is really wrong never matters before fixing something
options.outcome: Understanding what's really wrong actually matters a lot — it can save you from an unnecessary fix.

slides.title: Breaking it into smaller parts
slides.text: A big problem feels easier when you split it into smaller jobs. Instead of “clean the whole garage,” start with one shelf, then one box, then the floor.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to clean your whole messy room and it feels overwhelming. What's a smart first step?

options.label: Break it into smaller parts, like 'toys first, then books'
options.outcome: Exactly! Breaking a big task into smaller parts makes it feel much more manageable.

options.label: Try to do everything at once
options.outcome: Trying to tackle everything at once can feel overwhelming — breaking it into smaller steps usually works better.

options.label: Avoid starting since it feels too big
options.outcome: Breaking it into smaller parts is exactly what makes a big task feel doable instead of overwhelming.

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Good questions help you find useful clues. Instead of only asking “Why is this broken?”, ask “What happened right before it stopped working?”

widgetConfig.scenario: You're stuck on a problem. Instead of only asking 'why is this hard,' what's a more useful question?

options.label: A specific question that helps you find useful clues
options.outcome: Exactly! Good questions help you find useful clues, which is more productive than a vague 'why is this hard' question.

options.label: No question helps at all
options.outcome: Questions actually help a lot — a specific, well-aimed question can uncover useful clues.

options.label: Only vague questions are useful
options.outcome: Vague questions tend to be less helpful — specific questions uncover more useful clues.

slides.title: Brainstorming ideas
slides.text: Brainstorming means thinking of several possible solutions before choosing one. If you cannot reach a shelf, you might use a step stool, ask for help, or move the item to a lower place later.

widgetConfig.scenario: You can't reach a shelf. What's a smart first step before acting?

options.label: Think of several possible solutions, like a stool or asking for help
options.outcome: Exactly right! Brainstorming means thinking of several possible solutions before choosing one.

options.label: Just pick the very first idea with no other options
options.outcome: Picking the very first idea skips considering other options — brainstorming several first leads to a better choice.

options.label: Brainstorming several solutions never actually helps
options.outcome: Brainstorming several solutions actually helps a lot — it gives you more options to pick the best one from.

slides.title: Looking from a new angle
slides.text: When your first ideas are not working, look at the problem in a different way. Ask, “How would someone else solve this?”

widgetConfig.scenario: You've tried the same way to solve a puzzle three times and it's not working. What should you try?

options.label: Look at the puzzle from a totally different angle or approach
options.outcome: Great thinking! Trying a new angle can help you see solutions you missed before.

options.label: Keep doing the exact same thing
options.outcome: If the same approach hasn't worked three times, trying something different usually helps more.

options.label: Assume the puzzle is impossible
options.outcome: A new angle might reveal a solution — it's often too soon to assume it's impossible.

slides.title: Using tools to help
slides.text: Tools can make a solution easier and more accurate. A ruler helps you measure instead of guessing, and a checklist helps you remember steps.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to measure something accurately. What can help instead of guessing?

options.label: A ruler
options.outcome: Exactly right! Tools can make a solution easier and more accurate — a ruler helps you measure instead of guessing.

options.label: Just guessing with no tool at all
options.outcome: Guessing with no tool is less accurate than using a ruler to measure.

options.label: Tools never make a solution more accurate
options.outcome: Tools actually do make a solution more accurate, like a ruler helping you measure instead of guess.

slides.title: Naming the problem out loud
slides.text: A clear problem is easier to solve. “My science poster is hard to read because everything is crowded together” gives you more direction than simply saying “It looks bad.”

widgetConfig.scenario: Which description gives you more direction: 'it looks bad' or 'everything is crowded together'?

options.label: 'Everything is crowded together' — it is more specific
options.outcome: Exactly right! A clear problem is easier to solve — a specific description gives you more direction than simply saying 'it looks bad.'

options.label: 'It looks bad' is just as clear
options.outcome: 'It looks bad' is much less clear — a specific description like 'crowded together' gives you more direction.

options.label: A clear, specific problem statement never actually helps
options.outcome: A clear, specific problem statement actually helps a lot — it gives you real direction for solving it.

slides.title: Picturing the goal
slides.text: Picture what a good finished result should look like. If you are building a blanket fort, knowing you want space for two people helps you choose the right chairs and blankets.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're building a blanket fort for two people. Why does picturing this goal help?

options.label: It helps you choose the right chairs and blankets
options.outcome: Exactly right! Picture what a good finished result should look like — knowing you want space for two people helps you choose the right materials.

options.label: Picturing the goal never actually helps you plan
options.outcome: Picturing the goal actually helps you plan a lot — it guides what materials and choices you make.

options.label: You should never think about what the finished result should look like
options.outcome: Thinking about the finished result actually helps a lot — it guides your choices along the way.

slides.title: Checking your assumptions
slides.text: Sometimes your first guess about a problem is wrong. Check the simple possibilities first—for example, a slipping bike chain may just be loose rather than broken.

widgetConfig.scenario: A bike chain keeps slipping. Should you assume it's definitely broken?

options.label: No — check simple possibilities first, like if it is just loose
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sometimes your first guess about a problem is wrong — check the simple possibilities first, like a loose chain rather than a broken one.

options.label: Yes, always assume the worst right away
options.outcome: Assuming the worst right away skips checking simpler, more likely explanations first.

options.label: Checking simple possibilities first never actually helps
options.outcome: Checking simple possibilities first actually helps a lot — it can save you from assuming something is worse than it is.

slides.title: One clue at a time
slides.text: When you do not know the cause, test one possibility at a time. If the Wi-Fi is not working, checking the router first and then the device helps you learn which part is causing the problem.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your Wi-Fi isn't working. What helps you find the real cause?

options.label: Testing one possibility at a time, like the router first
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you do not know the cause, test one possibility at a time — checking the router first and then the device helps you learn which part is causing the problem.

options.label: Testing everything at once with no order
options.outcome: Testing everything at once with no order makes it harder to know what actually fixed it — testing one at a time is clearer.

options.label: Testing one possibility at a time never actually helps you learn the cause
options.outcome: Testing one possibility at a time actually helps a lot — it clearly shows you which part is causing the problem.

quiz.question: A toy robot won't walk. Why figure out the real problem first?
choices: So you know if it needs batteries or a real repair
Start taking it apart before checking simple causes
quiz.explanation: Figuring out the real problem first stops you from wasting effort fixing the wrong thing. Checking the batteries before taking a toy robot apart can save you a lot of extra work.

quiz.question: How can a huge job like cleaning a garage feel easier?
choices: Split it into smaller parts
Start everywhere at once instead of choosing one part
quiz.explanation: Splitting a big job into smaller parts makes it far less overwhelming. Instead of "clean the whole garage," try clearing just one shelf, then move to the next.

quiz.question: Instead of asking "why is this broken," what's a better question to ask?
choices: Ask a broad question without looking for clues
What changed right before it broke?
quiz.explanation: A sharper question points you straight to the answer instead of leaving you guessing. Asking what changed right before something broke often reveals the real cause faster.

quiz.question: What is "brainstorming"?
choices: Thinking of a few solutions before choosing one
Choosing before comparing other ideas
quiz.explanation: Brainstorming means thinking of several ideas, like a stool, help, or a broom, before choosing one. Comparing options usually works better than grabbing the very first idea.

quiz.question: Your toy sorting is stuck. What might help?
choices: Keep using the same sorting method even though it is not working
Imagining how someone very organized would do it
quiz.explanation: Looking at a stuck problem from a new angle can reveal ideas you'd otherwise miss. Imagining how a super organized friend would sort your toys might show a system you hadn't thought of.

quiz.question: Why measure wood with a ruler instead of guessing?
choices: It helps you avoid cutting the wrong size
Guessing is usually quicker than measuring
quiz.explanation: The right tool makes a tricky job easier and more accurate. Measuring wood with a ruler instead of guessing keeps you from cutting a piece the wrong size and wasting material.

quiz.question: Why is "my science poster looks messy" more useful than just feeling frustrated?
choices: It clearly names what actually needs fixing
Focus only on the frustration instead of naming what needs fixing
quiz.explanation: Naming a problem clearly helps you focus your effort on actually fixing it. Saying "my poster looks messy" points you toward a real fix, while just feeling frustrated does not.

quiz.question: Before building a blanket fort, why picture the finished fort first?
choices: It helps you know which steps actually move you toward it
Start building before deciding what you want to make
quiz.explanation: Picturing exactly what "finished" looks like helps you know which steps actually move you closer to it. Imagining the finished fort first keeps you from randomly grabbing pillows and chairs.

quiz.question: A bike chain keeps slipping. What should you check before buying a new chain?
choices: Assume the chain is broken before checking it
Whether the chain is simply loose
quiz.explanation: Checking your assumption first can save time and money before buying something new. A slipping chain might just be loose, not broken, so tightening it could be the whole fix.

quiz.question: Your Wi-Fi keeps disconnecting for an unknown reason. What's a smart approach?
choices: Check one possible cause at a time
Change several things at once so you cannot tell what helped

slides.title: Trial and error

options.label: Trial and error never actually helps solve a problem
options.outcome: Trial and error actually helps a lot — trying, adjusting, and testing again often leads to a solution.

slides.title: Learning from what didn't work
slides.text: A failed attempt gives you information. If your paper airplane keeps diving, notice what happened and change one part instead of making the same plane again.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your paper airplane keeps diving straight down instead of flying. What should you do?

options.label: Notice what happened and adjust your design
options.outcome: Exactly! A failed attempt gives you useful information — noticing what went wrong helps you improve your design.

options.label: Give up on paper airplanes entirely
options.outcome: Giving up skips the chance to learn from what happened — noticing and adjusting is how you improve.

slides.title: Testing your idea first
slides.text: Try a small test before doing a lot of work. Testing one paper airplane design before making ten can save time and paper.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to make ten paper airplanes of a new design. What should you do first?

options.label: Test one design before making ten
options.outcome: Exactly right! Try a small test before doing a lot of work — testing one paper airplane design before making ten can save time and paper.

options.label: Make all ten before testing anything
options.outcome: Making all ten before testing anything could waste time and paper if the design doesn't work — testing one first is smarter.

options.label: Testing a small version first never saves time or materials
options.outcome: Testing a small version first actually saves time and materials — it catches problems before you commit to all ten.

slides.title: Comparing your solutions
slides.text: When you have several ideas, compare them. Ask which one is safest, easiest, fastest, or most likely to work well.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have several ideas for a project. What helps you pick the best one?

options.label: Comparing which is safest, easiest, or most likely to work
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you have several ideas, compare them — ask which one is safest, easiest, fastest, or most likely to work well.

options.label: Picking randomly with no comparison
options.outcome: Picking randomly skips thinking about which idea is actually best — comparing them helps you choose wisely.

options.label: Comparing your options never actually helps you choose
options.outcome: Comparing your options actually helps a lot — it shows you which idea is most likely to work well.

slides.title: Solving problems with others
slides.text: Another person can notice something you missed. When building a tower, a friend may spot that the bottom is uneven while you are focused on the top.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're building a tower and focused on the top. What might a friend notice that you missed?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Another person can notice something you missed — while you're focused on the top, a friend may spot that the bottom is uneven.

options.label: Nothing — another person never notices anything new
options.outcome: Another person actually can notice something new, like an uneven bottom you missed while focused elsewhere.

options.label: Working with others never actually helps solve a problem
options.outcome: Working with others actually helps a lot — they can notice things you missed.

slides.title: Taking a break when stuck
slides.text: If you have been stuck for a while, a short break can help. When you come back, your brain may notice a clue or idea you missed before.

widgetConfig.scenario: You've been stuck on a tricky puzzle for 20 minutes and you're getting frustrated. What's the best move?

options.label: Keep pushing through the frustration without stopping
options.outcome: Pushing through frustration can make you more likely to make mistakes — a short break usually helps more.

options.label: Give up on the puzzle completely
options.outcome: You don't have to quit forever — a break, not giving up, is often all you need.

slides.title: Staying calm when frustrated
slides.text: Frustration can make it harder to think clearly. A slow breath, a sip of water, or a short pause can help you return to the problem with a clearer mind.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're getting really frustrated because your project isn't working. What helps most in the moment?

options.label: Keep pushing through the frustration without pausing
options.outcome: Pushing through intense frustration often leads to more mistakes — pausing to calm down first usually helps more.

slides.title: Bouncing back from a setback
slides.text: A setback is something that did not go the way you hoped. Instead of treating it as the end, ask what it taught you and what you can try next.

widgetConfig.scenario: Something didn't go the way you hoped. What's a helpful question to ask?

options.label: "What did this teach me, and what can I try next?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A setback is something that did not go the way you hoped — instead of treating it as the end, ask what it taught you and what you can try next.

options.label: Treat it as the end, with nothing more to learn
options.outcome: Treating it as the end skips a chance to learn — asking what it taught you helps you move forward.

options.label: A setback never actually teaches you anything useful
options.outcome: A setback actually can teach you something useful, if you ask what it taught you and what to try next.

slides.title: Knowing when "good enough" is good enough
slides.text: A solution does not always need to be perfect. If your tent is a little crooked but stays safe and dry, it may already be doing its job.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your tent is a little crooked but stays safe and dry. Does it need to be perfect?

options.label: No — it is already doing its job
options.outcome: Exactly right! A solution does not always need to be perfect — if your tent is a little crooked but stays safe and dry, it may already be doing its job.

options.label: Yes, it must be absolutely perfect
options.outcome: It doesn't need to be absolutely perfect — if it's safe and dry, it's already doing its job.

options.label: A solution never needs to just be "good enough"
options.outcome: A solution often can be just 'good enough' — it doesn't always need to be perfect to do its job.

slides.title: Checking in halfway
slides.text: For a long project, stop partway through and check your progress. Catching a mistake early in a Lego build is easier than discovering it after fifty more pieces.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're building a long Lego project. Why check your progress partway through?

options.label: Catching a mistake early is easier than fixing it later
options.outcome: Exactly right! For a long project, stop partway through and check your progress — catching a mistake early in a Lego build is easier than discovering it after fifty more pieces.

options.label: Checking partway through never actually helps
options.outcome: Checking partway through actually helps a lot — it catches mistakes while they're still easy to fix.

options.label: Mistakes are always just as easy to fix no matter when you catch them
options.outcome: Mistakes are actually much easier to fix early — catching them later, after more pieces are added, is harder.

quiz.question: A step stool doesn't reach, so you try a taller one. What is this called?
choices: Trial and error
Doing the same failed thing forever
quiz.explanation: Trial and error means trying something, checking if it works, and changing your approach if it doesn't. Trying a taller step stool after a short one fails is a perfect example.

quiz.question: A paper airplane keeps nose-diving because the nose is too heavy. Why does figuring that out help?
choices: It helps you avoid the same mistake next time
It's better to forget about it completely
quiz.explanation: Figuring out why something failed helps you fix it instead of repeating the mistake. Knowing a heavy nose makes a plane nose-dive tells you exactly what to change next time.

quiz.question: Why test one paper airplane design before making ten?
choices: It catches problems early and saves time
Testing first is always a waste of time
quiz.explanation: Testing a small version first catches problems before you've wasted a lot of time or materials. Trying one design before folding ten copies saves both paper and effort.

quiz.question: You have three ways to fix a wobbly table leg. What should you do?
choices: Just pick the first idea you had
Compare which is fastest, easiest, and works best
quiz.explanation: Comparing your options, like which fix is fastest or easiest, helps you choose the smartest solution. Grabbing the very first idea might not actually be the best one.

quiz.question: How can working with a friend help solve a problem?
choices: It can bring up ideas you wouldn't think of alone
It never helps at all
quiz.explanation: Working with a friend brings in a second set of eyes and ideas you might not think of alone. A friend might spot a wobble in your tower's base that you completely missed.

quiz.question: Why might a short break help with a tricky puzzle?
choices: Your brain can come back with a fresh idea
Breaks never help with anything
quiz.explanation: Stepping away from a hard puzzle for a few minutes lets your brain rest and reset. When you come back, you often notice a clue you missed the first time.

quiz.question: You feel frustrated because a problem is hard. What helps?
choices: Getting angrier at the problem
Taking a breath and staying calm
quiz.explanation: Feeling frustrated when a problem is hard is completely normal. Taking a breath and staying calm helps you think clearly instead of getting stuck in the frustration.

quiz.question: You lose the first round of a game. What's the most useful way to think about it?
choices: As a chance to learn the other player's strategy
As proof you should quit the game
quiz.explanation: Treating a lost round as useful information, not a disaster, keeps you moving forward. Losing round one might just mean you now know the other player's strategy for round two.

quiz.question: Your camping tent is a little crooked but keeps out the rain. What should you do?
choices: Accept it — it's a good enough solution for one night
Refuse to camp until it's perfectly straight
quiz.explanation: Not every solution has to be perfect to actually work. A tent that leans a little but still keeps the rain out is good enough for one night of camping.

quiz.question: Partway through a big Lego build, why pause to check your progress?
choices: It can save you from redoing work later
Checking partway through never matters
quiz.explanation: Pausing partway through a big project to check your progress can catch a mistake early. Stopping to compare with the instructions can save you from tearing it apart later.

slides.title: Breaking big problems into small ones
slides.text: A big, overwhelming problem becomes much more manageable once it's broken into smaller, clearer pieces you can tackle one at a time. For example, "plan an entire birthday party" feels huge, but breaking it into "pick a date," "make a guest list," "choose food," and "plan activities" turns it into four manageable tasks instead of one overwhelming one.

widgetConfig.scenario: 'Plan an entire birthday party' feels huge. What makes it manageable?

options.label: Breaking it into smaller tasks, like picking a date and guest list

options.label: Breaking a big problem into smaller ones never actually helps
options.outcome: Breaking a big problem into smaller ones actually helps a lot — it turns something overwhelming into manageable pieces.

slides.title: Weighing pros and cons
slides.text: When you have more than one possible solution, listing the good and bad points of each helps you choose more wisely than simply going with a gut feeling. For example, choosing between joining the soccer team or the debate club might come down to listing what you'd gain and give up with each — time commitment, what you'd learn, who you'd meet — rather than simply picking whichever sounds more fun in the moment.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're deciding between two project ideas and can't decide which one to pick. What's a smart way to decide?

options.label: Just pick randomly without thinking about it
options.outcome: A random choice might work out, but weighing the pros and cons usually leads to a better-informed decision.

options.label: Avoid deciding at all
options.outcome: Avoiding the decision doesn't solve anything — weighing pros and cons helps you actually move forward.

slides.title: Planning the steps
slides.text: Once you've picked a solution, mapping out the order of steps needed to do it makes the plan much likely to succeed. For example, if you decide to organize a class fundraiser, mapping out the order — get permission first, then plan the activity, then advertise it, then run it — keeps you from accidentally skipping something important like getting permission.

widgetConfig.prompt: You're organizing a class fundraiser — tap the steps in the right order

slides.title: Organizing your approach
slides.text: Writing down your plan, or listing the steps in order, helps you stay on track and notice quickly if something's been missed. For example, writing out "1) buy supplies, 2) make the product, 3) set up the table, 4) advertise" as an actual checklist makes it obvious if you forgot a step, instead of only realizing it halfway through.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have a big project with lots of pieces of information scattered everywhere. What helps most?

options.label: Organize everything into categories or a simple outline first
options.outcome: Exactly! Organizing scattered information makes a big project much more manageable to tackle.

options.label: Just start working randomly on whatever you see first
options.outcome: Working randomly on scattered information often leads to confusion — organizing first saves time overall.

options.label: Ignore the mess and hope it works out
options.outcome: Ignoring disorganization usually makes a big project harder, not easier — organizing first really helps.

slides.title: Generating multiple solutions
slides.text: Before settling on an approach, it's worth generating several different possible solutions rather than running with the first one that comes to mind. For example, if your school project needs a creative presentation, brainstorming options like a poster, a short video, a model, or a skit — before picking one — usually leads to a stronger final choice than committing to your very first idea.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your school project needs a creative presentation. What usually leads to a stronger choice?

options.label: Brainstorming several options before picking one
options.outcome: Exactly right! Generating several different possible solutions before settling on an approach usually leads to a stronger final choice than committing to your very first idea.

options.label: Committing to the very first idea that comes to mind
options.outcome: Committing to the very first idea skips considering other options — brainstorming several usually leads to a stronger choice.

options.label: Generating multiple solutions never leads to a better choice
options.outcome: Generating multiple solutions actually leads to a better choice — it usually produces a stronger final result.

slides.title: Setting a realistic deadline
slides.text: When planning the steps of a project, giving each step a rough deadline instead of a vague "someday" keeps a big task, like a science fair board, from turning into a last-minute scramble. For example, giving yourself Monday for research, Wednesday for the write-up, and Friday for the display keeps the whole project from piling up the night before it's due.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're planning a science fair board. What keeps it from becoming a last-minute scramble?

options.label: Giving each step a specific deadline
options.outcome: Exactly right! Giving each step a rough deadline instead of a vague 'someday' keeps a big task from turning into a last-minute scramble.

options.label: Leaving it all for 'someday' with no specific deadlines
options.outcome: Leaving it for 'someday' with no specific deadlines often leads to a last-minute scramble — specific deadlines prevent that.

options.label: Setting deadlines for each step never actually helps a project
options.outcome: Setting deadlines for each step actually helps a lot — it keeps a big project from piling up at the last minute.

slides.title: Must-haves vs. nice-to-haves
slides.text: When time is limited, separating what a solution absolutely needs from what would simply be a nice bonus helps you spend your effort wisely. For example, for a class presentation, clearly explaining the topic is a must-have, while fancy slide animations are a nice-to-have that can wait if time runs short.

slides.title: Choosing the right order

options.outcome: Exactly! Planning the right order prevents wasted effort and ensures each step builds properly on the last.

options.label: Order never matters as long as everything gets done eventually

options.label: You should always do the easiest steps first regardless of dependencies
options.outcome: Picking steps by ease rather than by what depends on what can create wasted, redone work.

slides.title: Setting a clear goal before planning
slides.text: Before mapping out steps, it helps to state exactly what "done" looks like, since a fuzzy goal makes it hard to plan clear steps toward it. For example, "raise $50 for the animal shelter" gives you a clear target to plan around, while "do a fundraiser" leaves you guessing what success even means.

options.label: A clear, specific goal never actually helps you plan
options.outcome: A clear, specific goal actually helps a lot — it gives you something concrete to plan steps toward.

options.outcome: Second opinions actually can catch something useful, like a gap you overlooked in your own plan.

options.label: It is always better to never show your plan to anyone else

choices: Choose more wisely between multiple solutions
Avoid ever making a decision

quiz.question: You decide to organize a class fundraiser. What should you do right after picking that solution?
choices: Just start advertising with no plan
Map out the order of steps, like getting permission first
quiz.explanation: Once you've chosen a solution, mapping out the order of steps keeps you from missing something important. Getting permission before advertising matters — skip that step and the whole plan could get shut down.

choices: It helps you stay on track and notice missed steps
Writing it down never actually helps

quiz.question: You're picking how to present a school project. What should you do before choosing?
choices: Brainstorm several different options first
Commit to the very first idea you think of

quiz.question: Why give each step of a science fair project its own rough deadline instead of a vague "someday"?
choices: Deadlines only add unnecessary pressure
It keeps the project from becoming a last-minute scramble
quiz.explanation: Giving each step its own rough deadline, like research on Monday and writeup on Wednesday, spreads the work out evenly. Without deadlines, a project can easily pile up into one stressful night before it's due.

quiz.question: For a class presentation, why is clearly explaining the topic a "must-have" while fancy slide animations are a "nice-to-have"?
choices: Animations always matter more than explaining the topic clearly
It helps you spend limited time on what actually matters most

quiz.question: Why can't you reasonably decorate a cake before you bake it?

quiz.question: Why is "raise $50 for the animal shelter" a better goal than "do a fundraiser"?

It gives you a clear target to plan concrete steps around

quiz.question: Why show your group project plan to a friend before starting?

Other people's opinions are never useful before starting

slides.title: Sticking with it through frustration
slides.text: Problem solving often gets frustrating before it gets easier. Pushing through that middle, frustrating part is often exactly what separates success from giving up. For example, learning a new skateboard trick often involves falling repeatedly and feeling frustrated right before you finally land it — that frustrating middle stretch is normal, not a sign to quit.

slides.title: Adjusting the plan

slides.title: Focusing on what you can control
slides.text: Some parts of a problem are out of your control. Focusing your energy on the parts you can influence tends to be much productive. options.label: Worrying about whether it will rain

options.label: Focusing on what you can control never actually helps
options.outcome: Focusing on what you can control actually helps a lot — it's more productive than worrying about things you can't influence.

slides.title: Testing your solution safely

For example, before committing to selling 100 friendship bracelets at a big school fair, testing the idea by selling simply 5 to classmates first can reveal pricing or design problems while the stakes are still small.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're considering selling 100 friendship bracelets at a big fair. What's a smart first step?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Trying a solution on a small scale first, like testing with 5 classmates, helps catch pricing or design problems before they get big.

options.label: Committing fully to 100 right away with no test
options.outcome: Committing fully right away risks bigger problems — testing on a small scale first catches issues while stakes are low.

options.label: Testing a solution on a small scale never reveals anything useful
options.outcome: Testing on a small scale actually can reveal useful things, like pricing or design problems, while stakes are still small.

slides.title: Pacing yourself on a long problem
slides.text: Big problems that stretch over days or weeks, like training for a tryout, go better when you pace your effort evenly instead of burning out in the first two days. For example, spreading practice across the two weeks leading up to a tryout works better than cramming every drill into the first weekend and having nothing left by the actual tryout.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're training for a tryout two weeks away. What works better than cramming everything into the first weekend?

options.label: Spreading your practice evenly across the two weeks
options.outcome: Exactly right! Big problems that stretch over days or weeks go better when you pace your effort evenly instead of burning out in the first two days.

options.label: Doing all your practice in the first two days
options.outcome: Doing all your practice in the first two days can lead to burning out — pacing it evenly across the two weeks works better.

options.label: Pacing yourself on a long problem never actually helps
options.outcome: Pacing yourself on a long problem actually helps a lot — it prevents burning out before the actual tryout.

slides.title: Recognizing when you're truly stuck
slides.text: There's a difference between a task simply being hard and an approach really not working at all, and noticing which one you're in tells you whether to push harder or change direction. For example, struggling to memorize lines for a play is normal and simply needs more practice, but reciting them the exact same way for a week with zero improvement might mean trying a different memorization method instead.

slides.title: Noticing small wins along the way
slides.text: Long problems can feel discouraging if you only judge yourself by the final result, so noticing small pieces of progress along the way helps keep you motivated. Stubbornly keep doing the same failing thing forever

Nothing is ever within your control

quiz.question: Why test selling 5 bracelets to classmates before committing to 100 at a big fair?

Testing small scale never reveals anything useful

quiz.question: Your debate partner might be absent on debate day. What's a smart move beforehand?

Prepare to cover both sides yourself just in case

Only the fully finished result ever counts as progress

Redesign the whole layout from scratch

slides.title: Checking if it actually worked
slides.text: After trying a solution, honestly checking whether it solved the problem — not simply whether it felt good to try — is an important last step. For example, if your new study method felt productive but your next test score didn't improve, honestly noticing that mismatch matters more than how the studying felt in the moment.

widgetConfig.scenario: A new study method felt productive, but your next test score didn't improve. What matters more than how it felt?

slides.title: Help isn't giving up
slides.text: Reaching out for help after really trying on your own is a sign of good judgment, not a failure to solve the problem yourself. For example, if you've spent real effort troubleshooting a coding project and you're still stuck, asking a teacher or looking up a forum post written by someone who solved the same issue is a smart, efficient next step.

slides.title: Reflecting on mistakes
slides.text: Looking back at what went wrong after a mistake, and being specific about it, teaches you much than simply feeling bad about it. For example, if a group project fell behind schedule, figuring out exactly where it slipped — was it unclear roles, or a missed deadline — helps you avoid the same slip on the next project.

options.label: Assuming mistakes teach you nothing
options.outcome: Mistakes can actually teach a lot — reflecting specifically on what went wrong is how you learn from them.

slides.title: Managing your time
slides.text: Solving a problem well often means managing how much time you spend on each part, instead of getting stuck perfecting one piece while ignoring the rest. For example, if you have a week to prepare for a debate, setting rough time limits for research, practice, and rebuttals keeps you from spending five days on research and only one day practicing.

options.label: Ignore the deadline completely

slides.title: Measuring success the right way
slides.text: Deciding upfront what "success" will look like makes it much easier to honestly judge afterward whether a solution worked. For example, deciding before a school clean-up event that success means "at least 20 bags of trash collected" gives you an honest way to measure it afterward, instead of simply guessing based on how the day felt.

options.label: Judging success should always just be based on how the day felt

slides.title: Trying again with a change
slides.text: If a first attempt falls short, trying again with one specific, intentional change is much useful than simply repeating the exact same approach and hoping for a different result. For example, if a lemonade stand made little money on a slow street corner, moving to a busier corner next time is a specific change worth testing, rather than simply setting up in the same spot again.

widgetConfig.scenario: A lemonade stand made little money on a slow street corner. What's smarter than just setting up in the same spot again?

options.label: Repeating the exact same approach and hoping for a different result

options.label: Trying again with a specific change never actually helps

slides.title: Keeping a simple problem-solving journal
slides.text: Jotting a quick note about what worked and what didn't right after solving something builds a habit of noticing patterns over time. For example, writing "starting my homework right after school works better than after dinner" after simply a few tries can turn into a really useful personal rule.

options.label: Turning a mistake into a rule never actually makes the lesson stick

slides.title: Separating effort from outcome
slides.text: Sometimes you do everything right and still don't get the result you wanted, and recognizing that your effort was really solid, separate from the outcome, matters. options.label: Effort and outcome are always exactly the same thing

slides.title: Time-boxing a tricky task
slides.text: Giving yourself a set amount of time for one part of a problem, instead of an open-ended amount, keeps you from spending your whole time budget in a single place. For example, setting a firm 20-minute limit for research on a report keeps you from accidentally spending three hours there and having no time left to write it.

Never ask for help under any circumstances

quiz.question: A group project fell behind schedule. What helps most afterward?

Just feeling bad about it and moving on

slides.title: A structured framework: define, plan, execute, review
slides.text: Many effective problem solvers follow a loose structure: clearly define the problem, plan an approach, execute it, then review what happened. For example, tackling a group project might mean first defining exactly what's due, then planning who does what by when, then doing the work, then reviewing afterward whether the plan worked well for next time.

slides.title: Root cause analysis
slides.text: Instead of treating symptoms, root cause analysis asks 'why' repeatedly until you reach the actual underlying cause of a problem, not simply its surface effects. For example, if you keep missing assignment deadlines, asking "why?" repeatedly might go: forgetting the due date → not writing it down → not having a consistent planner system — revealing that the real fix is a planning system, not simply "trying harder to remember."

options.label: Just keep fixing the symptom every time it happens
options.outcome: Repeatedly fixing just the symptom means the problem keeps coming back — finding the root cause is a more lasting fix.

options.label: Root causes never matter, only quick fixes do
options.outcome: Root causes actually matter a lot — without addressing them, the same problem tends to keep recurring.

slides.title: Deciding under real constraints
slides.text: Real-world problems often come with limits — time, money, resources. Good problem solving works within those constraints instead of ignoring them. For example, planning a class fundraiser with only $20 of seed money and two weeks of prep time means the solution has to realistically fit those limits, not assume unlimited time and budget.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're planning a class fundraiser with only $20 and two weeks. What should good problem solving do?

options.label: Assume unlimited time and budget
options.outcome: Assuming unlimited time and budget ignores the real constraints — good problem solving works realistically within them.

options.label: Real-world constraints never actually matter for a solution
options.outcome: Real-world constraints actually matter a lot — a solution needs to realistically fit the actual time and budget available.

slides.title: Prioritizing which problem to solve first
slides.text: When facing multiple problems at once, deciding which one to tackle first — based on urgency and impact — is itself an important problem-solving skill. For example, if you're behind on a homework assignment due tomorrow and also want to reorganize your room, tackling the urgent, high-impact homework first is the smarter priority, even if reorganizing feels more appealing right now.

slides.title: First-principles thinking
slides.text: First-principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic, undeniable facts and building a solution up from there, instead of simply copying how it's usually done. For example, instead of assuming a fundraiser has to be a bake sale because that's tradition, first-principles thinking asks what you need — attention and small donations — and then considers any way to get those two things.

options.label: What has always been done before, with no question

options.label: Breaking a problem down to basic facts never actually helps
options.outcome: Breaking a problem down to basic facts actually helps a lot — it can reveal solutions beyond just copying tradition.

slides.title: The "5 Whys" technique
slides.text: A structured way to perform root cause analysis is asking "why" five times in a row, since the fifth answer is often far closer to the true root cause than the first. For example, "why did I fail the quiz?" leads to "didn't study enough," then "why?" leads to "started too late," then "why?" leads to "no fixed study time" — eventually revealing a scheduling problem, not a knowledge problem.

options.outcome: The first answer is often just a surface symptom — repeating 'why' helps you dig down to the actual root cause.

options.label: Guessing randomly until something works
options.outcome: It's not random guessing — each 'why' is a deliberate step toward understanding the actual cause, not a guess.

slides.title: Defining success before you start
slides.text: Deciding in advance exactly what a successful outcome looks like prevents quietly redefining "success" after the fact simply to feel like you won. For example, deciding "improve my mile time by 30 seconds" before a training block begins gives you an honest, fixed way to judge the results later, rather than adjusting the bar afterward.

options.outcome: Deciding success in advance actually prevents something important — quietly redefining success just to feel like you won.

slides.title: Scoping the problem correctly
slides.text: A problem defined too broadly, like "fix my grades," is hard to act on, while one defined too narrowly, like "get one extra point on Tuesday's quiz," misses the bigger picture — good scoping finds a useful middle ground. For example, "raise my math grade this semester" is specific enough to plan around, without being so narrow that it misses the actual goal.

slides.title: Distinguishing symptoms from causes
slides.text: A symptom is the visible effect, while the cause is what's producing it underneath, and treating only the symptom never fixes the real problem. For example, a phone that runs slowly is a symptom — restarting it daily treats the symptom, but clearing out the too-many background apps causing it addresses the actual cause.
